Breaking: Lokomotive Leipzig, the 1987 Cup Winners’ Cup final and a rebirth from the ashes

📅 25 Jan 2022 | ⏱️ 8 min read (1560 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Thesefootballtimes

⏱️ ~8 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • In a recent development, picture the scene.
  • Recent findings suggest that they have seen bigger crowds than this here, of course.
  • According to recent reports, football is the one thing that the authorities cannot control, the rebellious child of the model socialist state.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, picture the scene. A communist-era colossus of a stadium, the vast expanse of concrete stretching as far as the eye can see, enclosing a seething mass of humanity, congregating in their blue and yellow scarfs. They will need them tonight, for this open bowl is completely at the mercy of the elements. The fans do not care, however. This is the Zentralstadion in Leipzig and it is about to witness its finest hour.

Recent findings suggest that they have seen bigger crowds than this here, of course. The Turn-un Sportfest, the socialist government’s regular celebration of athletic achievement, can draw attendances of 100,000 or more. This is the largest crowd it will ever see for a football match, though – and that matters.

According to recent reports, football is the one thing that the authorities cannot control, the rebellious child of the model socialist state. Football fans are not to be trusted; their first loyalty is to their teams and not to the party or the nation. They are prone to singing dissident songs and to bouts of hooliganism. Their unique culture is something that the state will never even try to understand. In these last years of the GDR, the terraces are also at the forefront of rebellion and change, operating, along with the church, as an open cover for opposition to one-party rule, hiding their protests in plain sight.

Sources indicate that they will say there were 74,000 people inside the Zentralstadion that night, but many more will claim to have been there. It seems apparent to even the most casual observer that the real attendance is close to touching six figures. Later estimates put the actual number at 120,000.

For the players who are about to step into this febrile atmosphere, this is their chance to make history. Lokomotive Leipzig are on the verge of reaching their maiden European final. They lead Bordeaux 1-0 from the first leg in France and now they stand 90 minutes away from the Cup Winners’ Cup final in Athens.

Lokomotive, the club, had already been through many incarnations. Their ancestors, VfB Leipzig, were the first national champions way back in 1903, when Germany was a unified nation. It is not apparent to those inside the ground tonight, but it soon will be again.

In a recent development, leipzig start the game with energy, flying into tackles, clearly fired up by the noise and passion of the crowd inside the stadium. It is Bordeaux, though, who take the early lead and go on to control the match.

Sources indicate that the home side continue to hold their own, however. They even have a chance to win the game late in the second half but Uwe Zotzsche’s penalty is saved by Dominique Dropsy in the Bordeaux goal. Extra-time is a tight affair and the match drifts to penalties.

Leipzig goalkeeper René Müller saves from Phillipe Vercruysse but Lok’s joy is short-lived as Matthias Liebers promptly sees his kick saved by Dropsy. Both teams’ penalty taking is unerring from that moment on, taking the shootout to sudden death. The tension in the ground is unbearable as Zoran Vujović steps up with the score tied at 6-6. His earlier goal has taken the tie this far but now he looks gripped by nerves.

Sources indicate that he hesitates twice on his long run-up before scuffing his penalty straight at Müller. The Zentralstadion erupts: Lok are now one kick from glory. Incredibly, the man stepping forward to take the crucial penalty is none other than Müller himself, the goalkeeper who now has the chance to score the most vital goal in his club’s history.

According to recent reports, müller places the ball and starts his run with a determined look in his eyes before blasting his penalty high into the roof of the net. He wheels away, arms in the air, and is instantly mobbed in a sea of exultant teammates.

According to recent reports, there is something symbolic about the celebrations inside the stadium. The fans don’t know it but this is as good as it will get for GDR football. Within two years, protests will begin in this very city, as young people craving the freedom of expression of Western society crowd onto the streets that surround the Zentralstadion. These protests will spread all over the nation, culminating in the fall of the Berlin Wall on a cold November evening. Within four years, the GDR will be no more.

So what became of Lokomotive Leipzig and those men in yellow and blue shirts? The team itself would go on to lose the Cup Winners’ Cup final to a dynamic Ajax side containing Marco van Basten, Frank Rijkaard and a young Dennis Bergkamp.

In many ways Lokomotive’s fate since that April night in 1987 mirrors that of the former GDR. Desperate to throw off the negative associations of communism and to seem at one with their fresh western countrymen, the team ditched the name Lokomotive in 1991 to become VfB Leipzig once again. A brief foray into the Bundesliga followed three years later before the economic reality of eastern life in the united Germany bit hard. By 2004, the club that had stood on the brink of European glory a mere 17 years earlier had ceased to exist.

In a recent development, the old Zentralstadion was a ruin, housing a shiny new ground inside its crumbling bowl. The new stadium was used during the 2006 World Cup in Germany and is now the home of RB Leipzig, the controversial franchise club owned by the Austrian soft drinks giant Red Bull. As an image of capitalism’s utter triumph over communism, only the McDonalds that now stands on Checkpoint Charlie is more symbolic.

It has been revealed that for many cities, this may have been the end of their famous old football club, but Leipzig is no ordinary place. The club’s fans rallied round and restarted Lokomotive Leipzig in the 11th tier of German football in time for the 2004/05 season. Fans rebuilt the club’s Bruno-Plache Arena brick by brick with their bare hands until it was fit to host football again.

Recent findings suggest that the response from the city was incredible. Lokomotive even broke the record for a lower-league football match in Germany when 12,421 spectators turned out for a game against Eintracht Grosbenden. The venue for this game? None other than the famous old Zentralstadion itself. The club that refused to die had come full circle.

It would be painting an unnecessarily rose-tinted picture to pretend that everything has been plain sailing since then. Leipzig’s tendency to be a microcosm of the eastern half of Germany has continued as the years have progressed. Lokomotive have not been alone in battling neo-Nazi hooligan elements as the far-right has sought to exploit the economic troubles and resentment of the former GDR for its own ends.

According to recent reports, the club has also failed to break out of the regional leagues despite plenty of near-misses over the last few years. However, the current picture is beginning to look altogether brighter. Leipzig is now an up-and-coming city, boasting a thriving tourism industry, trading in both shiny new architecture and GDR kitsch, or Ostalgia as it is called by locals.

According to recent reports, lokomotive, too, are on the up. The club has made commendable efforts to drive out the hooligan element and to make the Bruno-Plache a more welcoming environment for everyone. They boast one of their most impressive squads in recent years and harbour real hopes of soon returning to the Bundesliga structure.

Many lower league clubs have struggled to survive the empty stadiums, or “ghost games” as they are called in Germany, which have become a sad necessity of the COVID-19 pandemic. Lokomotive had their own unique solution to the problem. The club declared they would be selling tickets for €1 to a virtual game against the “invisible opponent” to raise money to pay the club’s 300 staff.

The aim was to set a new club attendance record, beating the 120,000 that were estimated to have been at the Zentralstadion for the Cup Winners’ Cup semi-final. Incredibly, Lok ended up selling 150,000 tickets for this imaginary game, the money keeping the club afloat through the months that followed. They do things differently in this unique city.

The joy of fans returning to stadiums this season has sadly been curtailed recently in the state of Saxony, where Leipzig resides, with matches temporarily being played behind closed doors once again. As a result, the Bruno-Plache Arena currently stands empty. Its last game with spectators was the derby against Chemie, another famous name from the GDR days. Lok won 1-0 in front of 6,000 passionate fans.

It has been revealed that those fans may be absent at the moment but soon they will return to cheer on the men in yellow and blue shirts, for nothing can quell their devotion. To this day, they still tend to their beloved stadium, picking weeds out of its’ cracks and painting its seats. It might not quite be the Zentralstadion on that magical night in 1987, but Lokomotive Leipzig and their fans are home again. Who knows, they may have a few more glory nights left in them yet.

By Billy Crawford @BillCrawford87.

Tech Report: Arsenal maintain perfect start but lack firepower of rivals

📅 31 Aug 2026 | ⏱️ 27 min read (5416 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Co

⏱️ ~27 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Bukayo Saka maintained Arsenal’s perfect start to the season, but Mikel Arteta appeared to acknowledge that the Premier League champions are in danger of leaving themselves short in attack.
  • There is still time for Arteta to add another forward to his squad and whether he does so or not could be key, with the transfer window closing on Tuesday night.
  • Having sold Leandro Trossard and with Gabriel Martinelli and Gabriel Jesus on the verge of moves away, Arsenal appear light of forward options.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Bukayo Saka maintained Arsenal’s perfect start to the season, but Mikel Arteta appeared to acknowledge that the Premier League champions are in danger of leaving themselves short in attack.

There is still time for Arteta to add another forward to his squad and whether he does so or not could be key, with the transfer window closing on Tuesday night.

Having sold Leandro Trossard and with Gabriel Martinelli and Gabriel Jesus on the verge of moves away, Arsenal appear light of forward options.

Lyon winger Malick Fofana has been offered to the club, but he is an underwhelming target given Morgan Rogers and Vinícius Júnior were pursued earlier in the summer.

According to recent reports, “We are trying to improve the squad,” Arteta, the Arsenal head coach, remarked. “Until Tuesday night, we’re going to try to do that. I’ve been disconnected from the world for 24 hours because I think my energy and focus has to be on the match. I will give it [my energy] now.”.

Sources indicate that asked if he currently has enough depth in forward positions, Arteta added: “It depends if everybody is fit or not. We know that the depth has to be really massive when you are fighting for four competitions. So we’re going to try to do that.”.

This was an Aston Villa team there for the taking after being gutted by their Premier League rivals and still waiting for newly introduced signings to be ready to play and gel.

But Arsenal made hard work of their victory and one senses there will be more games like this if Arteta has to rely on what he has already got until at least January.

Chelsea are showing they can score goals for fun having spent £117m on Rogers. Manchester City are strengthening their firepower with the signing of Iliman Ndiaye and Bradley Barcola has joined Liverpool. Arsenal have the defence and the midfield, but not necessarily the depth of quality in forward positions of their rivals.

0.52 - Arsenal faced the fewest shots (11), the fewest shots on target (1) and allowed their opponents the lowest xG (0.52) across the first two matchdays of the Premier League season.🔒 Locked. pic.twitter.com/blSUAeqoLb.

Christos Tzolis is the lone attacking signing to date and there was evidence at Villa Park that it will be a risk to rely too heavily on the Greek winger.

Tzolis had made an exciting start to his Arsenal career in the Community Shield and the first Premier League victory over Coventry City, but he had to be taken off at half-time on Monday night.

The former Club Brugge winger not only lost out to Matty Cash, but was also at the centre of Villa appeals for him to be sent off.

Tzolis had already been booked for a foul on Cash, when, in the 36th minute, he appeared to foul John McGinn as Villa broke from the edge of their own penalty area.

McGinn appealed that Tzolis should have been shown a second yellow card, but referee Jarred Gillett let the Arsenal man off the hook.

Arteta was wise to take Tzolis off at the break and his replacement, Eberechi Eze, had a hand in what proved to be Arsenal’s 59th-minute winner.

Industry observers note that eze slipped in Riccardo Calafiori and Saka got in front of Ian Maatsen to poke the Arsenal full-back’s low cross into the net. Saka’s goal had been the first shot on target in the game.

Industry observers note that "It's a brilliant goal, it really is" 👏 Bukayo Saka gives Arsenal the lead at Villa Park! pic.twitter.com/aV7DA8cARL.

Industry observers note that just before the goal, Arsenal thought they had been awarded a penalty. Ross Barkley lost possession with a sloppy pass, allowing Declan Rice to advance towards the Villa penalty area. He played the ball through for Saka and Maatsen barged into the back of the winger.

Gillett paused before pointing to the spot, but a VAR check revealed that Maatsen’s foul had taken place outside the penalty area and Martin Odegaard fired the resulting free-kick wide.

Sources indicate that the goal and the overturned penalty were pretty much it for Arsenal in terms of threatening the hosts, for whom goalkeeper Zion Suzuki made his debut. Suzuki did not have much to do with his hands, but impressed with his distribution.

It was Villa who went closest to scoring in the first half, through one of the club’s five surviving members of last season’s Europa League-winning team.

Emiliano Buendia scored Villa’s second goal in the final against Freiburg and the Argentine rattled the Arsenal crossbar with a 20-yard shot that had beaten visiting goalkeeper David Raya.

Before then, McGinn had sent a shot over Raya’s bar and into the building site where Villa are redeveloping the club’s old North Stand.

Buendia, McGinn, Cash, Pau Torres and Victor Lindelof are the only Villa players to have started the Europa League final who have not left this summer.

Defender Ezri Konsa is one of Villa’s Europa League winners to have departed and he made his Arsenal debut as a late substitute. The defender received a mixed reception, as he was first booed by some home fans but was then applauded.

Other than hitting the bar in the opening 45 minutes, Villa squandered a chance for a quick reply to Arsenal’s opener when McGinn hesitated instead of shooting after being played in by Nicolas Jackson.

Jackson lasted 71 minutes for Villa in what proved to be a promising debut. In the first half, he raced away down the right before sending the ball across the six-yard box. But there was no team-mate on hand to convert.

Recent findings suggest that one of Villa’s other summer signings, Alejandro Garnacho, is yet to make an impact for his latest club. The Argentine got an earful from manager Unai Emery for not being ready to go on. He eventually replaced Ross Barkley, but could not help conjure an equaliser.

Sources indicate that this is the start Arteta wanted. But, in attacking positions, Arsenal will finish the transfer window weaker than they started it if the club are not active in the final hours of the transfer window. And that could prove costly.

According to recent reports, we lost. We competed well. They won the league last year. We are trying to build a team but a lot of positive things [beyond] the result. How we competed. How it was progressively better. We didn’t create clear chances. Some players made fantastic debuts. Suzuki and Jackson did very good work. I think it’s the first step forward and positive for the next matches.

Accepting this result, I think we had chances to draw the match but we are in our rebuild. It is the way [ahead for us] making these changes and I say to the supporters and players that the message is there in the way we played.

To lose one match is painful but after the pain we must try to get positive things, This is the reason I am optimistic. There are 38 matches we played two. We haven’t one point but we can get better hopefully. And we will get players [Mbaye and Harwood-Bellis].

We can feel confidence because how we want to build the team again is true, to compete like today.

I think the squad we have now is how we planned with the  players we wanted.

[Are you confident you have replaced the quality that has gone?] Yes.

I’m really happy. It’s a massive win. It’s a tough place to come and earn the three points but I think we deserved it.

According to recent reports, it was a game where 11 was not enough and the finishers came in and did a magnificent job to win it. I know how tough it is to win here.

Every substantial team struggles against them for the past four years because they are so good. They are well coached, have great players. Great in transition. The moment you lose the ball and let them run inside they are really dangerous but I love a lot of the things I saw from my team.

Ebs [Eze] creates the action that sees us win the game, Bruno with Mikel [Merino] in midfield changed the dynamic of it, Ezri [Konsa] really composed and calm with every decision he made and then Zubi… I’m really happy with all of them.

Recent findings suggest that every game in the Premier League it’s like [you’re saying] we have to win this game. We know the level. We know how difficult it is in this league.

According to recent reports, [Can you sign Julian Alvarez tomorrow?] I don’t know. That’s for the people upstairs.

Recent findings suggest that it was a very tough match. Aston Villa’s defensive setup made things difficult for us, constantly catching us offside. We couldn’t attack as comfortably as we did last week. But as you know, sometimes one goal is enough for us. We have a very strong defence.

Today, we were great out of possession too and didn’t allow transition attacks.

Recent findings suggest that I keep my targets for myself. Every week I want to be there and try decide the game as that’s what I’m in the team to do. That’s my mentality.

In a recent development, [Have you seen Chelsea?] I’ve seen them. [What do you think?] We’ll see on Sunday.

Jamie Carragher explains how Arsenal broke Aston Villa down for their winning goal 🔎 pic.twitter.com/CAI8zhznrJ.

Recent findings suggest that arsenal host Chelsea on Sunday at 4.30pm while Villa go to Hull City at 5.30pm on Saturday. It’s too early for a must-win game for Villa who showed some positive signs tonight but they could certainly do with one.

Arsenal win with a performance of efficiency and patience that emphasises their superiority when asked to grind out a result.

John McGinnis arguing the toss with the referee about his belief that he was fouled in the box in the dying seconds. It was outside the box and if Maatsen’s ‘tackle’ wasn’t a foul, neither was Gabriel’s.

Not sure the way of refereeing that lets a lot of calls go and waits for VAR is going to enhance the game.

Maatsen tackles Bruno Guimaraes in the Villa box with an ugly lunge in which he appears to scissor him, kicking his heel with one leg before knocking the ball away with the other but the referee deems it fair and VAR lets it pass, too.

Arsenal’s game management is working well as usual until Raya goes too long and the ball bounces through to Suzuki. But when he starts a counter-attack Alysson ends it with a dive and back come Arsenal.

Industry observers note that maatsen slides in late on Saka down the right, bypasses the ball and crashes into his shin. Yellow card.

Aston Villa probe but Arsenal hold them 30 yards from goal and when they do slide pass down the side of a defender for Buendia to chase, Bruno is ideally positioned to cover and make the block which he celebrates as if he were Leonardo Bonucci.

Eight minutes of stoppage time are signalled by the fourth official.

Suzuki races 15 yards outside his box to head a long pass away from Havertz to McGinn. Back come Arsenal after McGinn is squeezed off the ball but Wan-Bisska wins it back with a fine tackle. He is among the best one-on-one pure defenders in the league.

Zubimendi rattles Buendia’s bones in a crunching but legal tackle.

Recent findings suggest that that was Rice’s last contribution as he limps off. He is probably OK but wise to withdraw him if he has had a twinge.

Maatsen drives down the left and cuts into the box. White leans into him, Rice guides him with a rigid left arm and the rampaging left-back loses his feet. Maatsen acknowledges Rice’s fine defending when he gets back up.

Quite a few outside observers questioned why Arsenal signed Konsa. This apparent injury to Mosquera is the reason. With Saliba out for months and Timber still struggling to regain his fitness, Mosquera was the only right-sided centre-back in the squad (unless they repurposed White, who is needed at right back).

Garnacho faces up Saka after being played down the left by Buendia but his cross is blocked by the goalscorer. Raya catches the resulting corner.

It has been revealed that mcGinn wipes out Merino from behind and is deservedly booked. Moments earlier Alysson was also booked for leaving one on Gabriel after the centre-half had cleared the ball, choosing not to put on the brakes and bodychecking him instead.

Unai Emery has just gone ballistic at substitute Alejandro Garnacho.

Emery clearly wasn’t happy with Garnacho not being ready to come on and let the Chelsea loanee know about it.

Garnacho → BarkleyWan-Bissaka → Cash.

And Mosquera cannot continue having overstretched so it’s a debut for the former Villa stalwart who is greeted warmly.

Suzuki saves in a one-on-one with Havertz running through from 40 yards, waiting and refusing to go down and make things easy for Havertz, sticking up a right arm to block the shot. But he may have been offside which may mitiagte it in terms of not costing Arsenal anything but he really should have beaten the keeper.

Nice pass from Merino to set the hare running.

Barkley plays a diagonal pass across the turf out to Alysson on the right and he hares round Calafiori to cross from the byline but could not get the ball past Gabriel at the near post.

Abraham → JacksonAlysson → Hemmings.

Bruno → OdegaardMerino → Lewis-Skelly.

Now Maatsen goes flying but this time in the Arsenal box under a challenge from White that was a duplicate of the one 30 seconds before. ‘Premier League corrupt as f---,’ sing the Villa fans, ignoring the similarities between the two incidents. The defenders’ arms made contact with the attacking players but without the force to send them sprawling.

Havertz hits the deck in the Villa penalty area when challenged by Kamara as they fought for Odegaard’s scooped dink from the right.

Bruno Guimaraes and Mikel Merino are stripped and ready to come on.

Industry observers note that once again, it’s Riccardo Calafiori who opens up the opposition’s defence with his off-the-ball running. He is the one player in this Arsenal team who makes genuinely unpredictable and unexpected movements.

McGinn’s combination with Jackson looks promising and the centre-forward invites him to bullock forward down the inside-right channel with a clever pass but the Villa captain is soon swamped by yellow shirts and the ball gets stuck beneath his feet.

Gary Neville makes the fair point that one of Arsenal’s most unheralded qualities is their patience. Their confidence in their rock-solid defence does not make them reckless but they are always confident of finding a way. They trust the method implicitly.

Aston Villa 0 Arsenal 1 (Saka) Mosquera has the ball 25 yards out, left of centre, he strokes it to Eze who angles a pass to Calafiori running between Cash and Lindelof. He makes it to the byline and cuts back a low cross that Saka and Maatsen both lunge at and the Arsenal winger gets there first to turn it in.

Industry observers note that "It's a brilliant goal, it really is" 👏 Bukayo Saka gives Arsenal the lead at Villa Park! pic.twitter.com/aV7DA8cARL.

Rice, Eze and Odegaard stand over it. Rive walks away and Odegaard approaches the ball with a semi-circular run-up. He whips it over the wall and about a foot wide of the left post. Suzuki was stranded but no matter.

It was outside the box. Not all that sure it was a foul either. But Arsenal will have a free-kick.

Recent findings suggest that maatsen and Saka collide as they chase a Rice pass that Saka would never reach. Seemed to be outside the box.

It has been fairly dull fare so far as two systems and structures that cede little space clash.

Lindelof rises high to meet Rice;s dipping cross from the right as Havertz, on his shoulder, was poised to pounce. He heads it straight up and Suzuki leaps to catch it.

According to recent reports, now Barkley picks out a diagonal to send Jackson down the left. The centre-forward reaches the 18-yard line, cuts inside and works it over to McGinn who lofts a cross over Villa’s back-post runners and out of play.

Industry observers note that eze did his best work from the left last season. Villa start with Barkley scoop-chipping a pass from the middle out to the left, 40 yards upfield. Maatsen runs on to it and drives past White to ram a shot into the side-netting.

Eze replaces Tzolis for Arsenal.

According to recent reports, arsenal were too slow to move the ball forward in that first half, and too loose with it when they did get into promising positions. There’s a lack of urgency in their passing. I wonder if we’ll see Bruno Guimarães soon… one of the reasons they signed him was to add more quick forward passing to their play.

Recent findings suggest that signs of encouragement for Villa without creating much while Arsenal have been stymied so far by Villa’s neutering of Tzolis and the left wing. Arsenal’s right-sided trio – White, Odegaard and Saka – look the most likely to create something.

According to recent reports, only a minute of added time to be played. Arsenal still lacking a spark, largely because there’s a lack of precision in their forward, line-breaking passing.

Recent findings suggest that villa will be very happy with this half. Much more like their old selves in terms of structure and organisation.

Calafiori’s throw to Gabriel is picked off by Jackson down the right and he dribbles down the right. He is forced to slow down to wait for a midfield runner. When Hemmings catches up, so have three Arsenal defenders and though Jackson bends in a low, cross to the edge of the six-yard box it is about 18 inches away from Hemmings’ reach.

Calafiori goes down in the Villa box when Pau Torres uses his arm to lever him away as they tracked the flight of a cross. The referee sees nothing wring in it and neither does VAR.

Sources indicate that gillett takes an age to stop the play when Cash uses his body to shove Tzolis over after the winger had played a pass. Cash obviously thinks he has rattled the new signing and is keen to rough him up some more. The ref does award a free-kick but only after that daft delay.

In a recent development, tzolis loses the ball on the edge of the Villa penalty area, tackled by McGinn. The captain slots a straight pass up to Buendia who tries to bend a pass into Jackson’s stride as he sprinted down the inside right channel but Gabriel read the trajectory and got there first.

Suzuki picks out McGinn with a long pass. He feeds it to Buendia who gives Hemmings a chance to chase it down the left. Arsenal shuffle over in defence so he doubles back and returns the ball to Buendia. The No 10 whips over a dipping cross looking for Barkley and Jackson but Calafiori and Raya make sure the goalkeeper wins it.

It has been revealed that we’ve not seen much from Christos Tzolis on Arsenal’s left wing so far. He’s been excellent since joining the club this summer but he’s hardly seen the ball in this opening half an hour and he’s just been booked after losing a battle with Matty Cash.

Arsenal free-kick 30 yards out, left of centre, for a foul on Lewis-Skelly who was artfully shielding the ball. Odegaard chips to the right post but Havertz heads it back across the box rather than going for goal and Villa clear.

It has been revealed that cash gets the better of Tzolis again in the tackle and then Suzuki sprays a perfect 60-yard pass out to Hemmings that Gary Neville, likening it to something Ederson was capable of delivering for Man City, one of the best goalkeeper passes he has ever seen. Tzolis was booked for stopping Cash running off with the ball.

Maatsen, who could never dislodge Digne for long, has a chance now to make the position his won. He strides down the left, exploiting Rice’s positioning error but his right-foot isn’t half as good as his left and his bending effort is scuffed far too straight and easily cleared.

Saka drives down the right after a neat Odegaard, Saka, White triangle. Pau Torres races over to toe the ball behind for a corner. Saka takes and Rice flicks it on at the near post and Suzuki tips it over. No corner, though, as Gabriel had rag-dolled McGinn at the back post after the Villa captain had backed in to him and tried to stop him making a run into the middle.

“Champions of Europe, you’ll never sing that.” Villa fans poke the wound.

Arsenal are finding it difficult to play through the middle of the pitch but have found Saka in space on the right wing on a few occasions already. Villa are congesting the central areas, where Odegaard does his best work.

In a recent development, calafiori picks off Kamara’s pass looking, for the third or fourth time, to play someone, usually Jackson, in behind the left-back. A minute later Calafiori challenges McGinn for a bouncing, loose ball and stoops to use his head. colliding with McGinn’s boot. Was the head low or the boot high? Arsenal think the latter but the ref sides, rightly, with McGinn.

According to recent reports, arsenal corner on the left. The threat inherent every time Rice is in a quadrant diminished on this occasion because Mosquera barged Cash just after Rice struck the ball. Free-kick to Villa.

Sources indicate that timber may be preferred by Arteta at right-back but Saka prefers White. The two have a well-grooved partnership in tersm of who underlaps and who overlaps. They never seem to get in each other’s way.

Bukayo Saka does seem to be getting a lot of time and space on the right flank.

It’s looking a risky tactic by Villa at the moment as the England international is being invited to cut in towards the penalty area.

Havertz is played down the inside-right channel in the penalty area by a cute Odegaard pass bur he blazes his shot across goal and wide of the left post. A replay shows he was offside but even so it was a lazy finish.

Kamara grabs Tzolis round the waist from behind and when the winger hits the deck, rounds him and passus to Buendia who crashes a right-foot diagonal shot on to the bar from 20 yards. The ref did not see it as a foul despite Arsenal’s protestations but had it gone in it would have given VAR a dilemma.

Worth keeping an eye on Aston Villa midfielder George Hemmings tonight.

He is only a teenager and has emerged from Villa’s academy, but Unai Emery is already a huge fan.

Hemmings produced a highly promising performance in the Super Cup against Paris Saint-Germain earlier this month.

Suzuki misjudges the flight of Rice’s typically menacing corner and flaps at it but his defenders and an offside flag leave him without egg on his face.

McGinn stops Calafiori down the left then gives the ball straight to Tzolis. The Greece winger opens his body and passes to Lewis-Skelly who shoots with his right foot from the left of the 18-yard line. Cash slides in to block the shot and it loops over the bar for a corner.

Hemmings uses his strength to hold off Ben White and shift the ball inside to McGinn who wraps his left instep around a shot and wafts it into building site behind Raya’s goal.

Ibrahim Mbaye and Taylor Harwood-Bellis are in the directors’ box watching the game. Villa don’t look like a hastily assembled team.

Suzuki knocks the ball long with his left foot, looking for Jackson but the ball spins away from him to Raya who boots it back upfield. McGinn pounces on it, turns past Rice and plays Cash in down the right. He crosses towards the near post and Mosquera hooks it clear.

Sources indicate that arsenal kick off with Odegaard spinning and trying to play Saka in down the right as they defend the empty North Stand end. The ball skids off the turf and Saka can’t trap it. The ball goes out for a Villa throw-in.

Who dies in the summer and played for both clubs.

In a recent development, arsenal are in fact in yellow and navy. My mistake.

Recent findings suggest that villa in claret and blue with a twist, the shorts are blue for the first time since, I think 2001. Arsenal are in yellow and black. Leeds, like Arsenal, have traditionally worn yellow and blue as their away strip but have been shunted into yellow and black as well by Adidas this season.

There are a few guys standing in the North Stand with hard hats on, and it appears they are on ball retrieval duty.

They will be on red alert for any wayward shots that land in the empty stand.

Warm reception for Ezri Konsa from Villa’s fans as he walked back to the tunnel with Arsenal’s substitutes.

Konsa joined Arsenal last week for £51m, ending a spell of seven years at Villa Park.

Good evening and welcome to live coverage of the Premier League match between Aston Villa and Arsenal from Villa Park. The champions travel to the team that finished fourth last season in buoyant mood and form despite some misgivings within their fanbase about their recruitment this summer.

It amounts so far to making Pier Hincapié‘s loan into a proper transfer, revamping the left wing with Christos Tzolis replacing Leandro Trossard and Gabriel Martinelli, upgrading options in central midfield by buying Bruno Guimarães and selling Cristian Norgaard – and signing Ezri Konsa from today’s opponents to give them the greatest elite defensive depth that I can recall at club since Manchester City’s Treble winners had Kyle Walker, Ruben Dias, John Stones, Nathan Aké, João Cancelo, Aymeric Laporte, Manuel Akanji, Rico Lewis and Sergio Gómez on the books at the same time.

It has been revealed that villa, by contrast, have endured a turbulent summer of trading with the departures of Europa League winners Morgan Rogers, Youri Tielemans, Lucas Digne, the aforementioned Konsa, Ollie Watkins and Emi Martínez, raising, along with other departures, more than £315m. They have spent about £180m to remodel the team though Johan Manzambi, who is injured, and João Gomes, who is suspended after his red card in the 4-0 defeat by Brighton, are absent tonight.

According to recent reports, we can expect to see Zion Suzuki, Matteo Ruggeri and hopefully Nicolas Jackson and Leon Goretzka who have been registered in time to play, plus the loan signings Aaron Wan-Bissaka and Alejandro Garnacho. Still to come are the pending purchases of Taylor Harwood-Bellis and Ibrahim Mbaye in a process that emphasises how profoundly Villa are invested in and dependent upon their manager, Unai Emery.

It has been revealed that after so much upheaval, it would be foolish to set much store on Villa’s 2-1 victory last season, sealed by Emi Buendía’s winner in the fifth minute of stoppage time. Arsenal barely broke sweat in blowing Man City away in the Community Shield and cakewalked to victory over Coventry in the league’s opening fixture. His past work suggests Emery will be able to forge another formidable side from his talented latest squad but this match feels two months too soon for him against his old club.

Edmundo: O Animal

📅 06 Feb 2022 | ⏱️ 12 min read (2361 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Thesefootballtimes

⏱️ ~12 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • It has been revealed that originally featured in the sold-out Brazil magazine, support high-quality, wholly independent journalism by ordering our magazine.
  • Industry observers note that A cauldron full of seething excitations: that’s how Sigmund Freud describes the id, the psychological structure responsible for our base desires.
  • In a recent development, his legend, like so many others of Brazilian football, began in the exacting slums of Rio de Janeiro.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that originally featured in the sold-out Brazil magazine, support high-quality, wholly independent journalism by ordering our magazine. It’s what keeps everything online free.

Industry observers note that A cauldron full of seething excitations: that’s how Sigmund Freud describes the id, the psychological structure responsible for our base desires. The id, Freud argues, must be kept in check to prevent man from acting impulsively against his own interests. A failure to repel one’s instincts, he warns, can have devastating consequences, not only for man but also his contemporaries. Nobody in football knows this more than Edmundo.

In a recent development, his legend, like so many others of Brazilian football, began in the exacting slums of Rio de Janeiro. Teixeira de Freitas Street may be just 30km from Ipanema, but for the downtrodden inhabitants of Niterói, it may as well be 3,000.

Whilst the Maracanã glistened across Guanabara Bay, Reinaldo de Souza was trying to raise a family. A barber like his father and brother before him, he struggled to make ends meet whilst his wife worked long hours as a cleaner. With nothing to distract them from the long period without their parents, brothers Edmundo and Luizinho passed their time like any other child in their street. Football became their home, and the pickup games on the beach became their education.

It was just as well for Edmundo, who highlighted no interest in academia. “Dinho”, as he was known to his family and friends, was focussed on one thing and one thing only. Even at a young age his talent was evident, a diminutive dribbler with a charring swagger, whose talent with the ball was matched only by the sharpness of his temper. He knew he was good and he wasn’t shy about it.

Industry observers note that it was his aunt who first spotted his talent. Maria had taken to minding the boys whilst their parents worked, and she would ferry Edmundo to practice and back as well as into the city to watch his beloved Vasco. It wouldn’t be long, though, before he graduated from fan to the first team. Aged 15, Edmundo was invited to trial with Botafogo’s youth wing. Fogão coach Tinoco knew genius when he saw it, and the youngster left Teixeira de Freitas behind for the big time.

Industry observers note that it’s at this point in the story where the prodigy defies the odds to succeed. But Edmundo’s tale isn’t one of romance or glamour, and it was at Botafogo that his nascent talent for self-destruction first became evident. With Maria struggling to afford the transport to and from the Botafogo facilities, Edmundo moved into the club’s youth lodging, but barely after joining he was expelled for walking naked through the grounds.

It has been revealed that luckily, Vasco didn’t mind exhibitionists. Perhaps they were swayed by an astonishing goal Edmundo had scored in a youth game in August 1991, where he had slalomed past an entire defence and goalkeeper before depositing a casual finish into an unguarded net.

In a recent development, after impressing for the reserves, Vasco coach Nelsinho gave him his debut in January 1992. The result, a 4-1 rout against Corinthians, augured well for a season in which the Vazcaínos would win the Carioca State Championship. Edmundo had been a revelation, dovetailing superbly with the mercurial Bebeto as his side finished third in the Brasileirão, but his strong personality led to continued clashes with his teammates.

The previous 17 years had been a disaster for Palmeiras fans. They had watched on trophyless as Corinthians and São Paulo won their first national and international titles respectively. In 1992, however, they would be rescued by the investment of the multinational conglomerate Parmalat.

According to recent reports, with Verdão surging thanks to Italian capital, coach Vanderlei Luxemburgo set about building one of the finest teams in Brazilian football history. Roberto Carlos, César Sampaio and Rivaldo were bright-eyed wunderkinds, but it was the capture of Edmundo for a record fee of $2m that captured fans’ imaginations. Vasco president Eurico Miranda was less than magnanimous, suggesting he was glad to get rid of a player who had been “a problem” for the dressing room.

Nevertheless, Edmundo would lead his fresh side to two straight Brasileirão titles and a State Championship. But “O Animal”, as he was christened by commentator Osmar Santos, once again found time to marry triumph with treachery. On 30 October 1994, São Paulo hosted Palmeiras at the Morumbi.

Like any Paulistano derby, it was a hot-blooded encounter, but both sides were resigned to a draw as the minutes ticked down. That was before Edmundo was on the receiving end of a particularly dodgy tackle near the touchline. Incensed, he raged at São Paulo coach Telê Santana on the bench, before seeking his retribution against striker Euller moments later.

A scrum ensued, with Edmundo punching André Luiz and slapping Juninho Paulista, prompting a full-scale fight between the teams in the process. By the time his teammate Antônio Carlos dragged him into the tunnel, six players had been sent off. Edmundo scored both his side’s goals that day, but nobody remembers them.

Sources indicate that it wasn’t the only sour note. The year before, he had been given a 40-day suspension for pushing a referee in the face, whilst he also found time to get into a fistfight with Antônio Carlos, the very man who had rescued him from the ravenous São Paulo players. Repeated fallouts with Luxembergo, meanwhile, were par for the course. Five red cards in one season spoke of a man seemingly incapable of self-restraint.

In 1995, he would even be detained by Ecuadorian police, his frustration at missing a penalty in the Copa Libertadores causing him to kick out at a local cameraman. It was only with the intervention of the Brazilian government that his release from the country was negotiated.

Despite winning everything with Palmeiras, the allure of Rio always held sway for Edmundo. In 1995, he joined a club that boasted 15 per cent of the country’s population as fans. Flamengo wanted to build an “attack of dreams”, with Dinho starting alongside Romário and Sávio as the club set their sights on continental domination.

Industry observers note that unfortunately they didn’t know how to defend, a leaky defence and problems off the field scuppering their chances. A terrible year was summed up in the most brutal of fashions when, during the 1995 Supercopa Sudamericana against Vélez Sarsfield, Edmundo was knocked out cold by a vicious punch from Flavio Zandoná. Except for Palmeiras fans, hardly anybody was sympathetic.

According to recent reports, off the field, Edmundo had endured a nightmare, but on 2 December 1995, his life descended into hell. After partying in a nightclub during the carnival, an inebriated Edmundo got into his Jeep Cherokee before driving straight into a Fiat Uno in the Lagoa suburb of Rio. The car, which had been travelling at 60mph in a 40mph zone, careened straight into a telephone pole. All three passengers died from their injuries.

According to recent reports, A tearful Edmundo was charged with involuntary manslaughter, whilst Flamengo tore up his contract. Not only did he face a possible jail sentence, but he also found himself without the one thing that had been constant in his life: football.

According to recent reports, it would be Corinthians who offered him hope just 45 days later. As Edmundo’s lawyers interceded on his behalf, his attempts to concentrate on football hit an immediate snag, with the striker walking out on the club before he had made a single appearance. Eurico Miranda, the man who had greeted his departure from Vasco with such disdain years earlier, successfully sought to bring him back home.

It was the best season of Edmundo’s career, as he broke the Brazilian scoring record with 29 strikes. His form was so impressive that some argued for his inclusion as a starter over Ronaldo for the 1998 World Cup, but coach Mário Zagallo resisted, citing his disruptive influence on the squad.

Despite a last-minute change of heart that saw him included in the final selection, Zagallo would be proven right. Edmundo would spend the entire tournament complaining about a lack of minutes, even contacting a Rio radio station to air his frustration publicly. When Ronaldo suffered a seizure before the final in Paris, Edmundo seemed to have finally been given his chance, only for the young superstar to emerge for the game amidst accusations of cover-ups and veiled suggestions of conspiracy.

Sources indicate that no matter. His 38 goals in 44 games had piqued Fiorentina owner Vittorio Cecchi Gori’s attention, and Edmundo was brought to Florence to augment one of Serie A’s most fearsome attacks. Alongside Rui Costa and Gabriel Batistuta, Edmundo would be charged with bringing domestic and European glory to La Viola. More importantly, though, it was a fresh start a thousand miles away from the flashbulbs and straplines of his home country.

Things went well at first, with the Brazilian combining lethally with Batistuta to fire his club to the top of Serie A. By the time Milan visited the Artemio Franchi in February, the home side had a chance to cement their lead, before Batistuta collapsed to the turf with an injury that would rule him out for two months.

Any normal footballer would have assumed the goalscoring mantle. Any footballer except for Edmundo would have been focused on delivering his team’s first Scudetto in 30 years. The Brazilian, however, was nowhere to be seen, having exercised a clause in his contract that allowed him to attend the Rio carnival back home.

Batistuta, like most of his teammates and the supporters, was incensed. “He was the right man if anyone wanted to have fun,” admitted the Argentine. “But to win something, he was not right.” By the time Edmundo returned to the club, his strikerless teammates had surrendered their lead, and would finish 14 points behind Lazio in third.

In each of his 18 months on the peninsula, Edmundo had made clear his desire to return home. When Eurico Miranda and Vasco called for him a third time, the transfer was as good as done. Back at his boyhood club and with the love of the fans behind him, Edmundo regained something close to his best form. The arrival at the club of Romário six months before the 2000 World Club Championship, however, reopened old wounds.

Industry observers note that the pair had been friends until 1998, before falling out after Romário’s beach bar in Rio was found to contain a derisory painting of Edmundo on one of the bathrooms stalls. When Romário refused to take it down, the pair fell out in spectacular fashion, so much so that when he joined Vasco, their relationship became a massive media circus. Their feud has been covered in excruciating detail in Brazil and beyond; suffice to say, these two giant talents and their commensurate egos found cohabitation difficult.

In a recent development, even the intercession of Vasco’s own priest, Padre Lino, couldn’t resolve their differences – not that Sir Alex Ferguson would have noticed. Romário and Edmundo combined with brutal efficiency to annihilate Manchester United in January 2000. After setting up Baixinho for the first, Edmundo had watched his partner capitalise on a second Gary Neville error to put the Brazilians two goals up.

It has been revealed that on 43 minutes, Edmundo joined in himself, scoring a goal that summed up everything about what made him a special, irascible talent. Receiving an innocuous ball from Gilberto on the edge of the box, Vasco’s number 7 spun Mikaël Silvestre with the outside of his right boot, before sliding a finish past a hapless Mark Bosnich.

It was a moment of pure relief. Three months earlier, Edmundo had been strongly criticised by animal rights campaigners, after he was pictured giving beer and whiskey to a chimpanzee at his son’s first birthday party. He’d also spent a night in jail as a result of his ongoing trial, before his lawyers intervened to appeal. If he was trying to stay out of the headlines he was doing a very bad job of it, but the goal against United ensured he would finally be making waves for the right reason. It proved to be a brief respite.

In a recent development, the “worst moment” of Edmundo’s career would arrive in the final of the same tournament, his missed penalty consigning Vasco to the runners-up medal at the hands of Corinthians. It was his last meaningful contribution at the highest level.

Brief but tumultuous spells at eight clubs – including a further two stints at Vasco and another at Palmeiras – followed, but Edmundo failed to recapture the violent genius that had been his unmistakable trademark.

It has been revealed that more tragedy would befall him in 2002, when his brother was found murdered in the back of his car in Rio. By the time the body was found, it was already in an advanced state of decomposition. Edmundo, overcome with grief, couldn’t bear to attend the funeral.

It has been revealed that in 2011, the shadow that had hung over Edmundo’s life for 16 years was lifted. Magistrate Joaquim Barbosa ruled that, in the case of the fatal car crash that had claimed three lives, the statute of limitations had expired. Edmundo was free, but the grief of the moment still lives with him every day. “I am an eternal repentant,” he admitted in an interview with Brazilian media. “This sadness does not pass.”.

There is no doubt that Edmundo’s career, with its litany of violent indiscretions and scurrilous headlines, makes less than pretty reading. But is he really, as one Brazilian journalist put it, “a liability to mankind”, or is he simply a deeply flawed human being, a man who struggled to reconcile a blessed gift with a cursed temperament? It’s a question that foregoes a simple answer. But what is simple is that Edmundo Alves de Souza Neto remains one of his country’s greatest talents. On the pitch at least, he is unassailable.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

von Next Generation am 22.09.2025 in den Kategorien Champions League mit 1 Kommentar.

Eintracht Frankfurt won their opening Champions League matchday with a 5-1 victory over Galatasaray Istanbul. After about ten minutes, Frankfurt were trailing 0-1, but thanks in part to adjusted pressing, they were able to turn the game around. What follows is an aspect analysis of Frankfurt’s attacking press against the Istanbul side’s build-up play.

It has been revealed that frankfurt started, as usual, in a nominal 4-2-3-1. Ahead of the two midfielders Chaibi and Larsson, Uzun operated in the No. 10 role. On the left flank, winger Knauff played in front of left-back Brown. When dropping into a deeper defensive press, this structure shifted into a 4-4-2, with Burkardt and either Uzun or Knauff forming the first pressing line. In the transition to the attacking press, they shifted man-oriented as usual.

Galatasaray also began in a nominal 4-2-3-1. In possession, their structure changed depending on the depth of their build-up, forming something like a 3-2-5 or 4-2-4 through the positioning of the full-backs. Width on the right side was provided by winger Sané, and on the left by full-back Elmalı. Left winger Akgün frequently moved inside, acting as a kind of “free player.” Meanwhile, right-back Sallai tucked in slightly in higher possession phases to help form a back three in the build-up.

Galatasaray’s build-up was characterized by frequent rotations. Their basic reference point was the previously described 3-2-5. From this shape, they consistently sought positional interchanges in order to manipulate the opponent’s man-marking in the pressing phase. On the left side, Elmalı, who provided width, was able to vary his height. In deeper build-up phases, he often dropped further back, while he also regularly positioned himself on the last line. Winger Akgün was tasked with creating central overloads and repeatedly moved inside, at times even drifting over to the right side. In response to the full-back pushing high, the left holding midfielder, Lemina, rotated into the left-back position. Striker Yılmaz, in turn, shifted into the left half-space when the full-back stayed deeper and the winger dropped centrally.

Galatasaray’s left-sided rotations force Frankfurt’s pressing players into constant reorientation.

Recent findings suggest that the purpose of these rotations was to manipulate man-marking and tie down specific Frankfurt players. Because winger Akgün frequently dropped into central areas, the two centre-backs, Koch and Theate, were occupied. Akgün positioned himself in front of striker Yılmaz in order to stretch the last line and create 1v1 opportunities. This produced a variety of different build-up structures, which required Frankfurt to constantly reorient themselves. For example, if Elmalı pushed high, he had to be tracked by Collins, and Galatasaray’s four attacking players tied down Frankfurt’s entire back line. This significantly complicated Frankfurt’s transition into man-marking, as the positioning of the forwards forced centre-back Theate to cover long distances during handovers.

Since all players in the back line are occupied, defensive handovers become more difficult.

Frankfurt’s proposal, as in previous matches, was to shift into man-marking from a +1 overload through the handover of the opponents’ centre-backs and full-backs. The advantage of this approach is that spaces on and behind the last line can initially be secured, while the risk of a long ball leading to a 1v1 situation is minimized by having an additional covering player.

At the same time, after steering the opponent’s attack, the transition into man-marking could be executed to apply maximum pressure on the ball carrier. Depending on the opponent’s structure and build-up sequences, Frankfurt adapted their pressing schemes. For instance, they could vary the distance to their opponents during the pressing jump: larger distances allowed for greater security in coverage, while smaller distances created more immediate pressure.

Galatasaray tried to make these handover moments as difficult as possible for Frankfurt by forcing the distances at the moment of transition into man-marking to become as large as possible. The aforementioned rotations, for example, forced Theate into long runs to pick up winger Sané, so that Brown could then jump out to the still unmarked and deeper-positioned right-back of Galatasaray.

Because of Galatasaray’s attackers’ positioning, Theate and Brown are forced into long pressing runs. On top of that, Theate finds himself caught between two opponents due to the rotations.

It has been revealed that galatasaray also tried to open up the center through certain rotations, aiming to draw Frankfurt’s midfielders out of central areas. Frankfurt tracked man-to-man with Larsson on half-space player Gündogan and Uzun on the deeper right-sided pivot Torreira. Depending on the side of build-up, Chaibi was prepared to jump onto the more advanced pivot, Lemina. Because Lemina often rotated into the full-back position, Doan frequently picked him up, leaving Chaibi or Collins (depending on the movements of Akgün and Elmalı) unexpectedly without a direct opponent. At the same time, Gündogan and Torreira sometimes rotated in opposite directions, which created difficulties for Frankfurt in terms of handovers in central areas.

Because Frankfurt found it increasingly difficult to press Galatasaray’s build-up through their usual handover approach, from around the 15th minute they opted for tighter marking distances to transition more rapidly into full man-marking. Brown pushed up directly, Theate went straight onto Sané, while Collins and Koch marked the two remaining forwards. This created a 3v3 situation on the last line. Although this increased the pressure on Galatasaray and led to more turnovers in their build-up, it also raised the risk against long balls due to isolated 1v1s. Time and again, Galatasaray managed to exploit this by sending strong dribblers like Sané into such spacious 1v1 situations. Even so, the tighter marking distances resulted in a much more balanced game with more frequent ball recoveries.

According to recent reports, in the 30th minute, Frankfurt used a longer stoppage to make more significant pressing adjustments. Winger Knauff no longer pressed Galatasaray’s right centre-back but instead oriented himself toward full-back Sallai. This allowed Brown to stay on Sané, and Theate no longer had to make long runs out wide to cover him. At the same time, it was no longer problematic if all four defenders were tied up, as they no longer needed to jump out of the back line. The free centre-back was now primarily pressed by Uzun, who used his cover shadow to block passing lanes into pivot Torreira. Galatasaray’s build-up on the right side could then be pressed man-to-man through ball-oriented shifting. To this end, Chaibi stepped onto Uzun’s original opponent, Torreira, and the far-side Doan also moved into the ball-near center.

Frankfurt’s pressing adjustments: With no need to shift across the last line anymore, Frankfurt gains situationally much better access with less risk. These changes spark the turnaround in the match.

Industry observers note that the pressing adjustments led to significantly better situational access and, at the same time, to much stronger defensive security. Frankfurt were able to use the resulting ball recoveries to establish longer possession phases, which gave them a more dominant style of play. One such spell of possession resulted in the 2-1 lead shortly before halftime. Immediately afterwards, a ball recovery from the adjusted attacking press led to a free kick, which in turn produced the 3-1 at the break.

In the opening 30 minutes, Galatasaray were able to cause Frankfurt problems, thanks in part to a very elusive build-up play that challenged Frankfurt’s typical pressing approach with its reliance on handover moments. Frankfurt’s adjustments, however, proved perfectly suited to applying pressure more easily while also improving defensive cover. The short interruption of play came at just the right time for Toppmöller and his coaching staff to implement the necessary measures. As a result, the pressing changes were decisive for Frankfurt’s eventual 5-1 victory and a successful start to their Champions League campaign.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Aaron Rodgers' recent comments about Mike McCarthy have drawn the ire of some of his former Green Bay Packers teammates. Former Packers offensive lineman T.J. Lang and former Packers receivers James Jones and Greg Jennings have publicly denounced Rodgers' treatment of McCarthy while taking their former coach's side following a chaotic 48-hour period in Pittsburgh.

Recent findings suggest that rodgers scorched McCarthy on "The Pat McAfee Show" on Wednesday, accusing his now-former coach of falling asleep at meetings, being late or absent from other meetings, not watching film in a timely manner and not developing a rapport with some of his players, especially the team's defensive players. Rodgers was benched after giving McCarthy an ultimatum: relinquish play-calling duties or release him. McCarthy benched Rodgers, and the Steelers released him after Rodgers publicly criticized McCarthy.

"I think it's despicable," Lang said on 97.1 The Ticket in Detroit. "I think that Aaron Rodgers just became everything that he has bitched about and moaned about over the last 10 years with former coaches, former teammates airing grievances out, giving opinions out in the media. He has blacklisted, I don't know how many former teammates from just simple comments telling the truth because he just he was sick of it.".

Lang, who spent eight seasons with Rodgers and McCarthy in Green Bay, noted that he is in a group chat with several former Packers who share his sentiment on the situation.

"I think it's just completely unnecessary," he noted. "I think it's victim mentality.".

TJ Lang on his former teammate Aaron Rodgers pic.twitter.com/0oiS3PybCn.

Jones, who also spent eight seasons with Rodgers and McCarthy in Green Bay, said he, too, is in a group text with former Packers teammates who don't agree with Rodgers' handling of McCarthy.

"How do you jump on Pat McAfee's show and say all this? Come on, man," Jones mentioned on the Speakeasy podcast. "My text thread is full of texts and group chats with a lot of my teammates right now, and none are on 12's side, especially the ones that know Mike.".

Jennings, who spent seven seasons in Green Bay and caught two touchdowns in the Packers' Super Bowl win over the Steelers, called Rodgers' decision to publicly air his grievances with McCarthy "distasteful." Jennings also criticized Rodgers for putting his former teammates in Pittsburgh in an awkward situation.

Industry observers note that "If you truly cared about more than just yourself, then you don't do this to everybody in that locker room that you just called brothers," Jennings mentioned on "First Thing First." "They are playing for something. You are no longer playing for anything.".

Industry observers note that @GregJennings weighs in on Steelers releasing former teammate Aaron Rodgers:“It was very distasteful… If you truly cared about more than just yourself, then you don’t do this to everybody in that locker room that you just called brothers... They are playing for something.” pic.twitter.com/whPyBO7K2p.

The general consensus among Rodgers' former Packers teammates is that Rodgers should have handled the situation behind closed doors, even if some of his accusations about McCarthy are true.

It has been revealed that "I don't even care if it's the truth," Jones stated. "Have the conversation with Mike in there. This is not something you go to the media bashing somebody. I would not do this to people that I love.".

The shaping of Thomas Frank and the early years at Brøndby

📅 14 Mar 2022 | ⏱️ 9 min read (1837 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Thesefootballtimes

⏱️ ~9 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • In a recent development, one of football’s feel-good stories in recent years has been the success of one-time minnows Brentford and Danish head coach Thomas Frank.
  • Frank himself is already being linked to bigger jobs, including Arsenal, and with his leadership style based on a close connection with his players and an emphasis on developing youngsters and previously under-performing stars, he is an incredibly likeable character who has become popular among football fans all over the world.
  • Industry observers note that however, before Frank moved to London in 2016 to join Brentford’s coaching team, he rarely looked like making it to the world’s biggest league.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, one of football’s feel-good stories in recent years has been the success of one-time minnows Brentford and Danish head coach Thomas Frank. Since being promoted from assistant manager to the hot seat in 2018, Frank has taken Brentford to latest heights, and capital side are currently punching way above their weight class in the middle of the Premier League.

Frank himself is already being linked to bigger jobs, including Arsenal, and with his leadership style based on a close connection with his players and an emphasis on developing youngsters and previously under-performing stars, he is an incredibly likeable character who has become popular among football fans all over the world.

Industry observers note that however, before Frank moved to London in 2016 to join Brentford’s coaching team, he rarely looked like making it to the world’s biggest league. In fact, failure was the word most associated with his career after a disastrous spell at Danish giants Brøndby.

Thomas Frank joined the yellow-blues as head coach in the summer of 2013 in the midst of a tumultuous time at the club. The job was his first as boss of a senior team, having previously coached youth teams. He did, however, enjoy success at under-16, 17 and 19 level with the national team.

During the 2012/13 season, Brøndby had only avoided relegation during the final set of fixtures, and were saved from bankruptcy at the eleventh hour when newly introduced ownership entered the club.

This meant that the club had to rebuild from scratch. Unable to compete with FC København financially, the previously successful youth department were to pave the long road back to the top of Danish football. With his experience as a youth coach and close relationships with several of the younger players, including Riza Durmisi, Frank was deemed the perfect candidate for the job.

In the years leading up to Frank joining the club, Brøndby had lost several promising talents to foreign clubs before they even made it in the first team. Andreas Christensen joined Chelsea, Pierre-Emile Højberg went to Bayern Munich, Patrick Olsen headed to Inter, Markus Bay and Nicolai Boilesen crossed to Ajax and Jannik Vestergaard joined Hoffenheim. This was a trend the board and Frank aimed at breaking.

The youngsters had to go all the way to the first team, partly to allow Brøndby to take advantage of their finest talents but also to ensure maximum profit from their inevitable sales.

And it wasn’t just empty words from Brøndby. Halfway through Frank’s first season, they introduced a latest and more ambitious academy under the name Brøndby Masterclass. Millions of kroner were invested and the club brought in new, foreign coaches to elevate the staff and knowledge base. The best example of this was the appointment of Albert Capellas, a former coordinator at Barcelona’s La Masia, as assistant coach to Frank, and the ideological cornerstone in the construction of the Masterclass.

Recent findings suggest that although ambitious, the new Brøndby board were patient. Having learned from the mistakes of the past, where expensive and underperforming signings, as well as frequent managerial changes, caused inconsistency, Frank was given unprecedented levels of trust.

Sources indicate that “It [the managerial changes] is over now. Development is our goal and is what we are keeping track of,” chairman Aldo Petersen mentioned shortly after Frank joined the club. “There won’t be changes just because our strategy isn’t going as hoped.”.

Petersen even guaranteed that Frank wouldn’t lose his job if the results were underwhelming for as long as he was chairman, and explained that he was ready to take a relegation to the second tier with Frank if he felt that they were still moving forward on the long-term strategy.

In a recent development, the trust was much-needed as Brøndby didn’t get the start to the season they wanted. Seven games into the Superliga campaign they were still without victory, and had been dumped out of the cup by a semi-professional team.

Reinforcements were obviously needed, and the board brought in established talent in club legend Thomas Kahlenberg and former Netherlands World Cup finalist Khalid Bouhlarouz, who strengthened a team that already had talented but inexperienced players such as Riza Durmisi, Kenneth Zohore and Christian Nørgaard.

The addition of the fresh players improved the level, and with better leadership on the pitch, results improved over the season as Brøndby finished fourth and qualified for European football for the first time in three years.

Halfway through the campaign, Jan Bech Andersen bought a controlling stake in the club and became the new chairman. The ownership also changed the ambition in the boardroom: instead of talking about development, processes and patience, the yellow-blues were now openly talking about titles and how to close the ever-growing gap to arch-rivals København.

Going into his sophomore year at Brøndby, which also happened to be the season that the club would celebrate its 50th anniversary, expectations grew. The young players now had a year under the belt as first-teamers, and Jan Bech Andersen splurged in the transfer window.

Sources indicate that brøndby broke the club’s transfer record when Daniel Agger returned home from Liverpool to finish his career, and with him came club legend Johan Elmander, who was a part of the 2004/05 double-winning squad under Michael Laudrup. Officially, the goal was to finish in the top three, but internally, the expensive, massive-name signings meant that the team should challenge for the title.

Sources indicate that the significant investment in the squad didn’t help much on the pitch, though. Brøndby were easily dismantled during Europa League qualification by a skilled Club Brugge side that won 5-0 on aggregate. At home, things weren’t much better.

Although Brøndby enjoyed an early-season victory at home against København, inconsistent results were commonplace. The team managed to play three games against newly-promoted Hobro IK, a semi-professional outfit with no prior Superliga experience, without winning. It negated all the good work against their biggest rivals.

Whilst it was clear that Frank wanted to control possession with his 4-2-3-1 formation, Brøndby barely created any chances. Even against the worse teams in the league, it was a fight to score goals, and when it happened, it often seemed like it was more down to the individual class of the players rather than the strategy working as intended.

On the sidelines, Frank often looked helpless, and while he was generally well-liked amongst the fans because of his communication skills and modern leadership style, cracks began appearing in the foundations.

Sources indicate that on the Sydsiden Stand, home of the most dedicated and vocal fans, the optimistic and cheerful Brøndby chants were slowly exchanged in favour of more pessimistic and negative tomes from the club’s tumultuous period of fighting relegation a few years earlier. Questions were raised about Frank’s ability to lead a major club like Brøndby and to motivate the experienced stars.

These questions became even louder during the winter break when Brøndby played a friendly against Hoffenheim in Germany. The Danes lost 7-0, while the press revealed that Frank needed advice from Agger on how to handle the embarrassment and punish the team, which damaged his standing among the players.

Industry observers note that after Agger retired, he spoke about the discussion he had with Frank on that day in Germany. ‘You know that we have spoken about consequences and those things. So what are you going to do now?’ he asked Frank. “We lost 7-0 and a lot of guys didn’t perform well enough. Maybe we aren’t in shape, but it was also mentally that we were wrong.”.

Industry observers note that agger suggested that Frank should call the players back to the training pitch during the upcoming days off. Frank was hesitant to follow the advice, seemingly unsure about demanding too much, to which Agger responded: “Of course you can. It is the only way people will understand. If I was coach, I would tell the players that they should show up in the morning. Only bring running shoes and we’ll go to the Brøndby woods.”.

Frank eventually followed the advice from his captain, but his soft style was not well-liked among the players, which Agger later spoke about. “As a person I really liked Thomas Frank, but as a coach, he wasn’t the one I liked the most,” Daniel Agger noted in 2017 when asked by Ekstra Bladet. “I am from the old school, where a football team has to be built around discipline and a hierarchy, but it wasn’t like that at all when I returned to Brøndby,” he recalled.

Brøndby went to finish third in the league, officially meeting the goal set out before the season, but it wasn’t in an impressive manor. The proud club finished 16 points behind FC Midtjylland and managed just 43 goals in 33 league games.

During the following season, Brøndby would once again depart the Europa League qualification in embarrassing fashion after a 6-1 defeat to Greek side PAOK.

In a recent development, in the league, things weren’t going much better. After finding themselves in the bottom half of the league, Frank’s troops went into the Christmas break in fifth place with all hopes of the title already washed away.

In a recent development, at this point, the support for Frank was reaching an all-time low. The offensive problems were deeper than ever despite the many significant names; millions of kroner had been wasted on players unable to reach their best under Frank. While there were still supporters calling for patience, more and more questions about Frank’s capabilities, or lack thereof, rose among both fans and pundits.

It was at this time, in the dark Danish winter days, a fresh account appeared on the Brøndby forum Sydsiden Online. Going under the username ‘Oscar’, it heavily criticised Thomas Frank and sporting director Per Rud with messages such as:.

In March, shortly after the spring season had started, it was revealed that the man behind the comments were none other than chairman Jan Bech Andersen himself.

Unsurprisingly, Frank decided to quit shortly after the news broke, leaving the club in fifth in the league following a 3-1 defeat to SønderjyskE.

Andersen himself was also forced to step down as chairman, but later regained his position, which he still holds this to this day.

According to recent reports, frank went nine months without a job following his exit before he joined Brentford as assistant coach in December 2016. While his stay at Brøndby never reached the expected heights, despite huge investment in the squad, there is no doubt that the experiences and chaos taught him about the tough world of professional football at the highest level.

Industry observers note that agger himself mentioned that he noticed how Frank became tougher on his players throughout the stay. Tactically, he also adjusted and clearly became more pragmatic, focusing on his opponents instead of stubbornly sticking to the same system. It’s all evident in his superb work at Brentford today.

#130554. Tech Report: The Issue of Passivity – MX
